title: Adaptive KV Sharding — meeting notes and design decisions
content:
Meeting: Adaptive KV Sharding — architecture review
Date: 2024-11-04
Facilitator: Aisha Rahman
Attendees: Aisha R., Marcus L., Evan M., Sofia N., Diego A., Priya K. (ops guest), Tom B. (benchmarks)
Location: Zoom / #eng-serving-runtime
Duration: 60m

Agenda
- Quick problem recap (5m)
- Proposed design overview (15m)
- Alternatives & tradeoffs (15m)
- Performance expectations & benchmark plan (10m)
- Migration strategy & rollouts (10m)
- Action items and owners (5m)

Problem recap
We currently use a static shard mapping for the KV prefix cache (per conversation). Static hashing causes hot shards for popular prefixes (e.g., short system prompts, common prefixes) and uneven memory consumption across GPU hosts. Hot shards lead to increased eviction churn, higher tail latency for cache hits, and poor tenant isolation under bursty workloads. The goal: design an adaptive sharding/placement layer that balances memory usage, reduces eviction churn, and supports multi-tenant isolation without needing full cross-host synchronous coordination.

High-level proposal (summary)
1) Logical shard layer: keep current per-conversation logical KV shards, but introduce an adaptive placement map that can move logical shards between physical hosts based on observed load and memory pressure.
2) Placement controller: a lightweight control plane process per-region (eventually HA) that monitors per-host memory, per-shard hit rate, and eviction rate. It issues placement hints and migration commands.
3) Lazy migration: when moving a shard, we copy the KV snapshot to the target and switch ownership via an atomic mapping update (no global stop-the-world). Readers route to new owner once migration completes; writers use versioned appends.
4) Soft affinity + replication: for extremely hot shards, create ephemeral read-replicas (read-only) to reduce tail latency while write path continues on primary. Replicas are created opportunistically and have TTLs.
5) Eviction policy: hybrid LRU + cost-priority (cost computed from recent hit-rate * token-length). Use per-shard budgeting rather than global LRU to maintain tenant isolation.

Design details discussed
- Placement controller metrics: host_free_mem_pct, per_shard_eviction_rate (evicts/min), per_shard_hit_ratio, average_seq_len, cpu_load for compaction tasks. Marcus emphasized sampling windows (1m/5m/1h) to avoid flapping.
- Mapping store: mapping must be consistent and low-latency. Proposal: store placement map in the region control-plane DB (etcd-like) with watch semantics; hosts subscribe to changes. We avoid heavy locking by introducing per-shard version numbers.
- Migration protocol: Diego walked through a 3-phase protocol: (1) allocate target slot and pull snapshot (2) apply a catch-up log for writes during copy (3) atomically swap mapping and drain source. We keep a bounded write buffer in the source to prevent data loss.
- Replica semantics: replicas are read-only caches kept in sync via the write-ahead log. Consistency model: eventual for reads; write paths always go to primary and acknowledgments are from primary. We accept small read-after-write staleness during migration windows.
- Memory accounting: use per-namespace quotas (tenant-level) and per-shard budgets to keep noisy-neighbor safeguards. Priya requested hard OOM protection that prevents a shard from exceeding precommitted GPU allocation. We added a plan to enforce soft memory caps via admission control at RPC gateway.

Alternatives and why rejected
- Global consistent hash ring with virtual nodes: simpler but doesn't adapt to hot spots quickly and requires rehashing which is expensive and high-churn during scale events. Rejected for tail latency concerns.
- Centralized in-memory index (single host) for hot prefixes: reduces duplication but creates a single point of failure and network hop for common ops. Rejected due to SLO risk for multi-tenant environments.
- Synchronous replication for hot shards: gives stronger read-after-write guarantees but significantly increases write latency and GPU-to-GPU traffic. We prefer async replicas with TTL.

Benchmarks and performance expectations
Tom presented preliminary numbers from microbenchmarks (local):
- Warm reads from local shard: p95 token latency 6.2 ms
- Remote shard read (no replica, over host interconnect): p95 token latency 9.7 ms
- Read from ephemeral replica: p95 token latency 6.8 ms (replica co-located on same rack)
Target goals for first rollout: average p95 token latency <= 10ms for typical chat workloads, reduction in eviction churn by >= 30% for skewed workloads, and < 1% request error increase during migrations.

Migration & rollout plan
Phase 0 — Experimentation (current)
- Implement controller in alpha mode (no automatic moves; only suggestions logged).
- Add telemetry hooks and dashboards (per-shard metrics).
Phase 1 — Opt-in migrations (canary hosts)
- Enable lazy migration for a small set of namespaces and non-critical tenants. Use manual gating via console.
Phase 2 — Auto-placement (gradual)
- Automatic moves based on thresholds with cooldown windows and rollback on SLO regressions.
Phase 3 — Replica autoscaling and heuristics
- System can create ephemeral replicas when hot-shard detection surpasses threshold and will tear them down after TTL or when hit-rate normalizes.

Operational considerations & risks
- Flapping: rapid move decisions could cause oscillation. Mitigation: hold windows, exponential backoff, and move quotas per-window.
- Networking load: snapshot transfers increase cross-host traffic. Mitigation: use rack-aware placement to favor local transfers and rate-limit snapshot copy.
- Consistency edge-cases: read-after-write during migration might see stale data. Acceptable for many LLM cache use-cases, but not for strict session state. We will surface a tenant-level opt-out for strict consistency (stick to static mapping).
- Complexity: adds control-plane components and more code paths. Plan to keep core runtime minimal and move complexity into controller service.

Decisions made (consensus)
1) Proceed with the adaptive placement design (controller + lazy migration) as the primary approach.
2) Use per-shard versioned mapping in a region control plane (etcd-backed). Hosts will subscribe to map changes.
3) Implement ephemeral read-replicas (async) for hot shards; no synchronous replication.
4) Eviction policy will be hybrid LRU + hit-rate cost and enforced with per-shard and per-tenant budgets.
5) Move forward with an opt-in canary rollout (Phase 1) before enabling auto-placement.

Open questions (to resolve in follow-ups)
- Exact snapshot transfer format: raw KV binary vs compacted delta. (Action: Marcus to prototype both.)
- Admission control thresholds and default budget sizes per-tenant. (Action: Priya + Product to propose defaults.)
- How to expose migration telemetry in Console (events vs metric series). (Action: Sofia to draft console UX.)

Action items
- Marcus: prototype snapshot delta format and cost model for transfer (due 2024-11-18).
- Tom: run rack-aware vs random-host copy benchmarks and report p50/p95/p99 (due 2024-11-14).
- Evan: start controller skeleton and mapping store integration (PR skeleton by 2024-11-11).
- Sofia: mockups for console migration dashboard and per-shard view (due 2024-11-13).
- Priya: draft tenant budget default proposal and risk policy (due 2024-11-15).
- Diego: write up migration protocol state machine and failure/retry semantics (due 2024-11-12).

Notes & follow-ups
- Next architecture sync scheduled: 2024-11-18 10:00 PT to review Marcus prototype and Diego state machine doc.
- Keep linked RFC updated: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/SRV/Adaptive+KV+Sharding+RFC
- Related tickets: INF-3482 (placement controller), SERV-1291 (replica orchestration).

Appendix (short sketches)
- Shard mapping example: namespace: conv-12345 -> host-a (v3) -> replica host-c (ro, ttl=10m)
- Migration failure handling: if target copy fails 3x, mark shard sticky to source for 15m and alert SRE.

End of notes.

Document owner: Aisha Rahman
Reviewed-by: Marcus Li, Evan Martinez
